reason: Each spoken claim has a direct NPS or Library of Congress source, with exact excerpts and caveats in research.md; this editorial correction requires a new render and review.
story: Sitting Bull’s vision of falling soldiers is described by NPS and LOC. On June 25, 1876, Custer’s Crow scouts located a large Lakota and Cheyenne village. Fearing the village would scatter, Custer advanced and divided the 7th Cavalry. Reno’s attack failed. Custer ordered Benteen forward with ammunition, a message written by adjutant W. W. Cooke. Benteen followed Weir north after joining Reno, but Lakota and Cheyenne warriors forced them back. All 210 men in Custer’s five-company battalion were killed. The broader battle continued into June 26.
angle: Custer’s call for Benteen to bring ammunition did prompt an attempted move north; Lakota and Cheyenne warriors forced the troops back.

claims.claim: NPS and LOC describe a vision in which Sitting Bull saw soldiers falling into his camp before the battle. Present this as a reported vision, not a proven prediction.
Custer and the 7th Cavalry approached the Little Bighorn village in June 1876; the battle began June 25.
Custer’s Crow scouts located the large Lakota and Cheyenne village. NPS estimates the village population around 8,000.
Custer feared the village would scatter when he thought his regiment had been detected, and ordered an immediate advance.
Custer divided the 7th Cavalry into three battalions under himself, Reno, and Benteen, with an additional pack train.
Reno’s attack on the southern end of the village failed and his battalion retreated to the bluffs.
At Custer’s order, W. W. Cooke wrote a message for Benteen: “Come On. Big Village. Be quick. Bring Packs. P.S. Bring packs.”
After joining Reno, Benteen followed Weir north toward Custer, but approaching Lakota and Cheyenne warriors forced the troops back.
Custer led five companies comprising 210 men; all men in his immediate battalion were killed. The wider battle lasted into June 26.

disputed: No direct NPS/LOC passage checked here establishes that scouts told Custer the village was too large to attack or that he ignored their warning; those lines and the old title were removed.
The chronology gives no one-hour duration for the death of Custer’s battalion; “in an hour” was removed.
NPS says Reno and Benteen attempted to move north and were driven back; “help never arrived” and “neither moved” were removed.
Cooke wrote the Benteen message for Custer; the quote card now credits Cooke.
The vision is a reported account and is not stated as a supernatural fact.

The original topic prompt called the village the largest Native American encampment ever gathered on the plains; the checked NPS/LOC sources give a large estimated population but do not verify that superlative, so it is excluded from the revised story.
